title: Clustering revealed a high-risk churn group — target it with an intervention?

scenario.role: You're the growth analyst at Quillwork
scenario.situation: Data science clustered accounts on session_length_min, actions_per_session, and exports_count and found 3 distinct groups. Devon, the head of Growth, is treating one cluster as a "newly discovered at-risk group" and wants to build a dedicated re-engagement email flow around it, separate from the existing trial/paid lifecycle emails.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: "The clustering found a real at-risk group we didn't know about. Let's build a new re-engagement flow specifically for it."
scenario.question: Is this cluster actually new information — or is it just account_status (trial / expired_trial / paid, already in the CRM) wearing a data-science label? Check whether the cluster tells Devon anything he didn't already know before a new email flow gets built around it.

columns.name: account_status
columns.description: expired_trial, trial, or paid — already tracked in the CRM

columns.name: session_length_min
columns.description: Average session length in minutes — gated by account status usage limits

columns.name: actions_per_session
columns.description: Average actions taken per session — gated by account status

columns.name: exports_count
columns.description: Exports in the last 30 days — export is a paid-only/limited-trial feature

columns.name: onboarding_completion_pct
columns.description: Percent of the onboarding checklist completed (0-100), not gated by account status

columns.name: retained_90d
columns.description: 1 if the account was still active 90 days later — the outcome a re-engagement flow should be targeting

columns.name: cluster
columns.description: K-means(k=3) cluster label from clustering on session_length_min/actions_per_session/exports_count (standardized)

guidingQuestions: Cross-tab cluster against account_status. How closely does each cluster line up with a single status?
Group by account_status and separately by cluster, and compute retained_90d in each group. Does either one meaningfully separate who's retained?
If cluster and account_status tell you almost the same thing, what does a 'new at-risk group built from the cluster' actually add over what's already in the CRM?
Now correlate onboarding_completion_pct with retained_90d, and compare that to how well account_status or cluster predicts it.
If Devon wants a genuinely new, actionable re-engagement signal, which column should the new flow actually target?
suggestedApproach: Cross-tab cluster vs. account_status and note how tightly each cluster maps to one status — or compute an agreement metric directly.
Compute the retention rate within each account_status group, then within each cluster group, and compare — are either of them differentiating?
Name the mechanism: session_length_min, actions_per_session, and exports_count are all gated by account status by product design, so clustering on them can only rediscover status.
Correlate onboarding_completion_pct (a column not used in the clustering) against retained_90d, and compare the strength of that relationship to account_status's.
Recommend where the real signal is, and what a genuinely new re-engagement flow should be built on instead of the cluster.

notebook.intro: Five steps: check what the clusters actually are, whether they differentiate anything, and where the real retention signal lives.

cells.title: Cross-tab the clusters against account status
cells.explain: Before treating a cluster as a discovery, check whether it is a column you already had.
cells.code:
table = pd.crosstab(df["cluster"], df["account_status"])
agreement = table.max(axis=1).sum() / len(df)
print(f"each cluster is {agreement:.1%} explained by a single account status")
table
cells.reads: The clusters map almost one-to-one onto account status. Nothing new has been found.

cells.title: Ask whether either one differentiates
cells.explain: Compute retention within account status and within cluster, and compare.
cells.code:
by_status = df.groupby("account_status")["retained_90d"].mean() * 100
by_cluster = df.groupby("cluster")["retained_90d"].mean() * 100
print("retention by account status (%)")
print(by_status.round(2))
print("retention by cluster (%)")
by_cluster.round(2)
cells.reads: Both give the same split, because they are the same split.

cells.title: Name the mechanism
cells.explain: The clustering inputs are gated by account status by product design. Look at how they move across statuses.
cells.reads: Each input is largely determined by status, so clustering on them can only recover status.

cells.title: Look at a column the clustering never saw
cells.explain: onboarding_completion_pct was not used to build the clusters. Check how it relates to retention.
cells.code:
df["onboarding_band"] = pd.qcut(df["onboarding_completion_pct"], 5, labels=False, duplicates="drop")
by_onboarding = df.groupby("onboarding_band")["retained_90d"].mean() * 100
print("retention by onboarding-completion band (%)")
print(by_onboarding.round(2))
print("correlation with retention:")
print(round(df["onboarding_completion_pct"].corr(df["retained_90d"]), 3))
cells.reads: The ignored column separates retention sharply, and it is something a re-engagement flow could actually act on.

cells.title: Where the real signal is
cells.explain: Compare the spread in retention each variable produces.
cells.code:
status_spread = by_status.max() - by_status.min()
onboarding_spread = by_onboarding.max() - by_onboarding.min()
pd.DataFrame(
    {"retention spread (pts)": [status_spread, onboarding_spread]},
    index=["account status (what the cluster found)", "onboarding completion (what it ignored)"],
).round(2)
cells.reads: Targeting the cluster targets the billing state you already know. The actionable signal was left out of the model.

teachingNote.naiveRead: The clustering surfaced 3 groups data science hadn't explicitly labeled before. One reads as "at risk," and it feels like a genuine discovery worth building a dedicated flow around.
teachingNote.theTrap: session_length_min, actions_per_session, and exports_count are all directly gated by account_status — expired trials are capped hard, active trials are capped moderately, paid accounts have full access. Clustering on three columns that are themselves consequences of account status can't discover anything account_status didn't already tell you: the cluster label matches account_status with an adjusted Rand index of 0.999, essentially identical. And crucially, neither account_status nor the cluster predicts who's retained 90 days later — the retention rate is flat at about 20-22% across every status and every cluster. The "newly discovered at-risk group" isn't a discovery; it's expired_trial wearing a data-science label, and it doesn't even predict the thing Devon wants to act on.
teachingNote.honestAnswer: Don't build a new flow around the cluster — it's redundant with account_status, which is already in the CRM. The real, non-redundant signal was sitting in a column the clustering didn't use: onboarding_completion_pct correlates with retained_90d at about 0.34, meaningfully higher than anything account_status or the cluster offers (both ≈ 0 lift on retention). Tell Devon: skip the cluster-based segment, and instead target accounts with low onboarding_completion_pct for the re-engagement flow — that's the genuinely new, actionable signal, not something the lifecycle emails already segment on by status.
howToGetThere: Cross-tab or compute adjusted Rand index between cluster and account_status: ≈ 0.999 — essentially the same variable.
Compute retained_90d rate by account_status and by cluster separately: both flat at ≈ 20-22% — neither differentiates who's retained.
Name the mechanism: the three clustered features are all status-gated by product design, so clustering on them can only rediscover status.
Correlate onboarding_completion_pct (not used in the clustering) against retained_90d: ≈ 0.34 — a real, independent signal.
Recommend targeting onboarding_completion_pct directly for the new re-engagement flow instead of the redundant cluster.
teachingNote.lesson: Clustering on features that are themselves downstream of a variable you already know can only rediscover that variable — it isn't a new segment just because a model produced it. Before calling a cluster a "discovery," check its agreement with variables you already track (status, tier, plan) and check whether it actually predicts the outcome you care about, not just whether it looks different in a chart. The real signal is often sitting quietly in a column nobody clustered on.
